newsitem.title: UK: British jobless falls to lowest since 1990.
newsitem.headline: British jobless falls to lowest since 1990.

text.p: British unemployment fell to its lowest level in almost seven years in April, but the new Labour government immediately announced plans to review the much-criticised figures to make them more credible.
The Office for National Statistics said Wednesday that unemployment fell by 59,400 to 1.65 million in April, the lowest total since August 1990, for a jobless rate of 5.9 percent.

Underlying average earnings grew by a slower-than-expected 4.5 percent in the year to March, compared with a 5.0 percent rise in the year to February, suggesting a slight easing in inflationary pressures.
The government, which had derided the jobless data as "fantasy figures" while in opposition, welcomed the fall in unemployment but said it was time the figures were overhauled.
This is a bold move as most economists argue that any serious review of the way unemployment is measured will probably show that many more people are out of work.
"Credibility must be restored to the official unemployment statistics. The public have suspected they have been the object of political manipulation," said Employment Minister Andrew Smith.
The ONS said it would consult economists, statisticians and the media about how best to present the figures and hoped to bring in any changes by late summer.

Britain is unique in calculating unemployment as the number of people out of work and eligible to claim benefits. Regular changes to the criteria for eligibility have led to major distortions in the data.
Many economists would like Britain to adopt the widely recognised International Labour Organisation measure of unemployment as the number of people out of work and looking for a job.

A recent independent study by Sheffield Hallam University calculated that real unemployment in January was more than double the official 1.8 million figure. This would represent an unemployment rate of around 13 percent, roughly in line with rates in other key European countries such as Germany and France.
Economists said the move to review the statistics was very welcome and long overdue.
"We have been living with manipulated, distorted data for 15 years," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International.
Economists agreed that despite flaws in the series, unemployment was clearly falling quickly.
